title: batchSize
sub: What the second number in Schedule means, light work versus heavy, work stealing, and the Timeline instead of guessing
cards/0/title: batchSize — how many iterations per grab
cards/0/body:
Parallel scheduling takes two numbers: the length and the batchSize — the second argument of IJobParallelFor.Schedule(length, innerloopBatchCount, dependsOn) and IJobFor.ScheduleParallel(length, innerloopBatchCount, dependsOn). The range 0..length is cut into batches of batchSize iterations.

A thread takes a whole batch and runs its Execute calls back to back, in a tight inner loop. In the words of the docs, a value of 32 means the job queue steals 32 iterations and then performs them in an efficient inner loop.

A batch is indivisible: one thread runs it. So no more threads can work at once than there are batches.
cards/1/body:
The batches are spread over several native jobs — roughly one per worker thread. Whoever finishes their own first steals from a neighbour: according to Unity’s docs, half of its remaining batches at a time, so that neighbouring data stays with one thread (cache locality).

Grabbing a batch is an atomic operation. So small batches balance the load better, but they are not free: every batch costs an atomic and a start of the inner loop.
cards/1/flow/2: ran dry → steal half from a neighbour
cards/2/q: 1000 elements, batchSize 500, the machine has 8 worker threads. At most how many threads run this job at the same time?
cards/2/explain: 1000 / 500 = 2 batches. A whole batch runs on one thread, so at most two work in parallel and six sit idle, however many cores there are.
cards/2/wrong/1: Eight threads could work if there were at least eight batches. There are two.
cards/2/wrong/2: There would be one batch with a batchSize of 1000 or more.
cards/2/wrong/3: batchSize is the batch size in iterations, not a thread count.
cards/3/body:
Light work is a couple of multiplies and adds per element: move a particle, add two vectors. An iteration costs nanoseconds, comparable to grabbing a batch. Unity recommends 32–128. With a batchSize of 1, the overhead of grabbing every single iteration eats the gain.

Heavy work is pathfinding, tree traversal, hundreds of operations per element. Here the grab is cheap and the danger lies elsewhere: one big batch of expensive elements lands on a single thread and everyone waits for it — a long tail. Unity recommends a small batchSize, down to 1, especially when the cost per element is uneven.

And check the batch count: length / batchSize should be well above the number of worker threads, or some threads sit idle and stealing has nothing to share.
cards/3/deep: If you want to handle a batch yourself, Collections has IJobParallelForBatch: Execute(int startIndex, int count) receives the whole batch. Inside you can keep one scratch buffer per batch instead of one per element, or write a loop that is easier to optimise.
cards/4/q: Match the situation with the conclusion
cards/4/pairs/0/1: 32–128: an iteration is cheaper than grabbing a batch
cards/4/pairs/1/0: Pathfinding for 300 agents, costs vary a lot
cards/4/pairs/2/1: One batch — one thread does the work
cards/4/pairs/3/1: The grab overhead eats the gain
cards/5/body:
The numbers from the docs are a starting point, not the answer. The answer is in Profiler → CPU Usage → Timeline: it shows the worker threads and the slices named after your job.

  • A long tail: one or two threads are still computing, the rest are empty — the batches are too big, or the expensive elements ended up in one. Lower batchSize.
  • The job gets longer as you lower batchSize — the per-batch overhead now outweighs the work itself. Raise it.
  • WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread — the main thread is waiting for the job in Complete(). That is a signal not about batchSize but about collecting the result too early, or a job too long for the frame.

The method from the docs: start at 1 and increase until the gain becomes negligible. Measure on the target hardware, ideally in a development build: a phone and your workstation have different core counts.
cards/6/q: You are looking at the Timeline. What is true? Select all.
cards/6/options/0: One thread computes the job for a long time while the others are empty — lower batchSize
cards/6/options/1: WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread means the main thread is waiting for a job in Complete()
cards/6/options/2: With 8 worker threads, batchSize should be length / 8
cards/6/options/3: A good batchSize is the same on every device
cards/6/options/4: If the job got longer when you lowered batchSize, the per-batch overhead won
cards/6/explain: A tail points to batches that are too big or uneven; time growing with small batches points to overhead. WaitForJobGroupID shows a wait in Complete(). One batch per thread leaves no slack for stealing: as soon as one thread is busy elsewhere or gets the expensive elements, everyone waits for it. Devices have different core counts, which is why batchSize is checked on the target hardware.
cards/7/task: In Crowd both jobs (IJobFor) are scheduled with a poor batchSize. MoveJob moves 100,000 particles — a couple of operations per element: use a value in the 32–128 range. PathJob finds a path for 200 agents and the cost varies a lot: use 1. Both jobs stay on ScheduleParallel; do not add Complete() to Update.
cards/7/checks/2/label: There is no Complete() in Update
cards/7/explain: With batchSize 1 the light MoveJob has 100,000 batches and as many grabs for next to no work. With 256, all 200 PathJob agents fall into one batch, and a single thread does all the pathfinding. After the fix, check the Timeline: MoveJob’s threads finish almost together, and PathJob has no lonely tail.
cards/8/q: Interviewer: “What batchSize do you usually use?”
cards/8/options/0: It depends on the cost of an iteration: 32–128 for light work, down to 1 for heavy, uneven work. Then I check the Timeline on the target hardware
cards/8/options/1: Always 64 — that is the value from the docs, so that is what people use
cards/8/options/2: Always 1: that balances the load best
cards/8/options/3: The element count divided by the core count — exactly one batch per thread
cards/8/explain: A good answer names both ends, explains why (grab overhead versus the tail) and ends with a measurement. “I tune batchSize from the Timeline” sounds like experience; a single number sounds memorised.
cards/8/wrong/1: 64 is a reasonable start for light work, but pathfinding for 200 agents is then only four batches: at most four threads work, and one expensive batch makes a tail.
cards/8/wrong/2: On light work, batchSize 1 spends more on grabbing batches than on the work itself.
cards/8/wrong/3: One batch per thread leaves no slack for stealing: one expensive chunk or one busy thread and everyone waits.
